claims.text: An atomistic simulation explicitly incorporating oxygen-induced defect scattering will predict electrical conductivity more accurately than traditional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The proposed accuracy advantage will hold in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The modeled material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Enhanced DFT or parameterized interatomic potentials can be used to model oxygen-defect scattering in this alloy.
Experimental conductivity measurements already exist for an approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimen in both stated temperature windows.
Oxygen impurity sites act as scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen scattering centers modify electron transport relative to an ideal defect-free lattice.
Oxygen scattering centers modify phonon transport relative to an ideal defect-free lattice.
At 0–200 K, enhanced impurity scattering reduces conductivity relative to defect-free predictions.
At 300–1200 K, oxygen introduces additional phonon scattering and defect–lattice interactions.
Traditional analytical models fail to capture the non-ideal conductivity behavior caused by oxygen defects.
The proposed model will predict reduced conductivity in the 0–200 K regime.
The proposed model will predict a distinct, experimentally consistent conductivity trend in the 300–1200 K regime.
The proposed model will closely match measurements on oxygen-containing samples and outperform perfect-crystal predictions.
The comparison baseline consists of analytical predictions for perfect, defect-free bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The model's proposed applicability is limited to specimens with oxygen levels near 1 wt.% and temperatures within 0–200 K or 300–1200 K.
Predictions for other oxygen concentrations or temperatures outside the stated windows remain uncertain.
Variability in oxygen spatial distribution and local environment can affect the magnitude of the conductivity change.
Oxygen impurity distribution can be characterized using methods such as TEM or XPS.
A discrepancy greater than 20% between measured and modeled conductivity in either temperature regime is designated as the falsification threshold.

contradictions.description: The core hypothesis is comparative—greater accuracy than existing analytical models—but the falsification experiment does not require predictions from the analytical baseline. A greater-than-20% error would not by itself disprove comparative superiority if the baseline error were still larger, and an error below 20% would not establish superiority.
